beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Adwait Changan, and this video is about what happens after a reviewer asks a finance agent to go back and check its work. This week I built the re-investigation loop. Three follow-up requests went in. Three different answers came out, and only one of them was yes. That is the whole point.

props.command: A reviewer sends work back. What does the system actually re-check, and what can it refuse?

Every specialist result is replayed and compared, not trusted.
Three requests went in: one verified, one unsupported, one still open.

beats.narration_text: A follow-up only means something if it points at a specific earlier run. So every request is bound by hash to the exact investigation it is questioning. If the routing plan changed, the run is rejected. If the underlying trend log changed, rejected. You cannot quietly re-open a different investigation than the one the reviewer looked at.

beats.narration_text: Here is that replay, eighteen lines. Re-hash the plan. Re-hash the trend log. Then re-run the entire orchestration from scratch and compare the fingerprint of every specialist result against what was stored. Four separate conditions in there end the run. Notice it never reads the old answer and agrees with it. It regenerates the answer and checks whether it still matches.

beats.narration_text: Now, the reviewer sends three different kinds of request. Verify what you already have. Test this explanation I think is true. And go find evidence that does not exist yet. A system worth trusting has to answer those three differently.

props.title: Three Requests, Three Answers

beats.narration_text: And it did. Verify existing evidence came back verified, because the replay matched exactly. Test causal claim came back unsupported, because nothing in the evidence establishes the cause. Request additional evidence stayed open, because the operational records simply are not there. One yes, one no, one not yet.

beats.narration_text: That middle row is the one I would check first if someone handed me this system. A review loop that can only ever return verified is not reviewing anything. It is a rubber stamp with extra steps. This one rejected a causal claim that a reviewer proposed, and it left a third request unfinished rather than closing it.

props.caption: The replay matched exactly, and closure is still blocked. Those are different things.

beats.act: ACT 3 — WHAT VERIFIED DOES NOT MEAN
beats.narration_text: And here is the sentence I care most about in the whole report. Verified means the evidence replayed exactly. It does not verify a business cause. Those are completely different claims, and the gap between them is where a finance tool either stays honest or quietly starts lying to people.

beats.act: ACT 3 — WHAT VERIFIED DOES NOT MEAN
beats.narration_text: Which is why the loop is fenced on five sides. A modified source file is caught. A missing task is caught. A duplicate request is refused. A citation pointing at evidence that does not exist is refused. And a report that was overwritten after the fact is detected rather than absorbed.

props.caption: Each one ends the run rather than being absorbed into the result.

beats.act: ACT 3 — WHAT VERIFIED DOES NOT MEAN
beats.narration_text: The output is an append-only closure pack. Before and after, side by side, for every task. Nothing is edited in place, so a reviewer can see what changed and what did not. And closure status stays blocked pending human review, because the system finishes the checking and stops exactly where judgement begins.

beats.act: ACT 3 — WHAT VERIFIED DOES NOT MEAN
beats.narration_text: The easy version of this feature returns verified on all three and closes the ticket. That version would have been faster to build and completely useless to a reviewer, because a result that is always yes carries no information at all.

beats.narration_text: So, the verdict. A reviewer can now send work back, and each follow-up is bound by hash to the exact investigation it questions. Every specialist result is regenerated from scratch and compared by fingerprint rather than trusted. Three requests produced three different answers: one verified by exact replay, one causal claim rejected as unsupported, and one left open because the operational evidence does not exist. The replay matched exactly and closure is still blocked, because verified means the evidence replayed, not that anyone has established a cause. Final approval stays with a named human reviewer.

artifactLines: Every follow-up is bound by SHA-256 to the exact investigation it questions.
Specialist results are regenerated and compared by fingerprint, never read and trusted.
Three requests, three answers: 1 verified, 1 unsupported, 1 still open.
Five refusal paths: modified source, missing task, duplicate request, unknown citation, overwritten report.
Replay was EXACT_MATCH and closure is still BLOCKED. Verified means replayed, not explained.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Take a system I have built that re-checks its own work and tell me every outcome it is capable of returning. If the only outcome is success, explain what that costs a reviewer who is relying on it. Then show me the smallest change that would let it return an honest no. Run that on something you own. If you cannot find the path that produces a refusal, you have not built a check. You have built a formality.

props.command: Take a system I have built that re-checks its own work. List every outcome it is capable of returning. If the only outcome is success, explain what that costs a reviewer relying on it. Then show me the smallest change that would let it return an honest no.
output: If you cannot find the code path that produces a refusal, it is not a check.
A checker that always passes is indistinguishable from no checker at all.

beats.narration_text: That was Reviewer-Guided Re-investigation and the Closure Pack for the Mycroft Finance Investigator. The code and the full before and after report are in pull request seventeen. Adwait Changan, for Humanitarians AI.
